questions.answer: Importance of the location as a major hub for bioinformatics and life sciences, with a strong research environment and internationally recognized institutions

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was a relatively easy process. We had online sessions to guide us through all the required paperwork, and although there was quite a lot of bureaucracy, these sessions were very helpful.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Online sessions before the stay. On site we didn't have any particular assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Although there was no specific on-site assistance upon arrival, the online preparation sessions were very helpful. They made sure we knew what to expect, how to navigate the main practical matters, and who to contact if we needed support.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: They offered Erasmus accommodation in dormitories managed by Studierendenwerk Heidelberg, which we could apply for, and I was fortunate to receive a place, as they are pretty competitive (especially because they are pretty affordable). Since I went to Heidelberg to complete my MSc thesis, I was not attending courses but working at the research group where I carried out my thesis project. The dormitory I was assigned to was therefore extremely convenient in terms of location.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
I lived in a two-bedroom apartment, and the kitchen was probably the least convenient part. It was very small, with space for only one person to use it comfortably at a time, and there was limited storage.
On the other hand, Heidelberg University provided access to cafeterias, or Mensas, across the campus. There was usually one nearby, which made finding affordable and convenient meals very easy.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: On-campus housing can be very convenient in terms of location and affordability, however, facilities can be quite basic, and shared spaces may be small.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was somewhat challenging to adjust at first. Since I was conducting research for my MSc thesis, I was in a working environment rather than attending classes with other students. I think being in classes would have provided more opportunities to meet people and make friends, so building a social network required a bit more effort.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
One of the main challenges was that people often seemed quite reserved, and in some situations they preferred to speak German even when they were able to communicate in English. This sometimes made it more difficult to feel included.

I would also have appreciated the opportunity to take a German language course before going on exchange. At UCPH, the available German courses were taught in Danish, which was not suitable for me as a non-Danish speaker. I therefore took a German course in Heidelberg instead. However, it was still challenging to practise the language with native speakers while I was only beginning to learn it.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I particularly appreciated the food. I was pleasantly surprised by the quality and variety, both in restaurants and in supermarkets. I found it easy to access good food and enjoyed trying different local products and dishes.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
-If you are going during the summer, be prepared for the heat. Heidelberg can get extremely hot, and when I was there in summer 2026, very few university buildings had air conditioning. I only had a fan in my room, and it was not enough, so I would strongly recommend getting a portable air conditioner if possible.
-Make an effort to explore Heidelberg and join social activities, even if you are going alone. Since I was working on my MSc thesis rather than attending classes, it was much harder to meet people naturally, and I ended up spending less time exploring the city than I would have liked. I wish I had pushed myself a bit more to go out, discover the city, and attend activities on my own.
-Eat as much Flammkuchen as you can.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part was the research experience I gained while working on my MSc thesis. The project may contribute to a publication in a strong scientific journal, which would be an important outcome of the exchange and a valuable addition to my academic CV.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The greatest challenge was the combination of the summer heat and the social isolation. Since I was working on my MSc thesis rather than attending classes, I had fewer natural opportunities to meet other students and make friends. I often felt homesick and found it difficult to build meaningful connections during most of my stay.
